name: Armeria gRPC server (Java): grpc_bench unary echo vs C++ gRPC (cpp_grpc_mt)
baseline: gRPC C++ async server with one completion queue and one thread per CPU (cpp_grpc_mt in LesnyRumcajs/grpc_bench), built with g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto and linked with jemalloc
workload: grpc_bench complex_proto unary RPC echo (the handler copies the request field into the reply), ghz client with 50 connections and 1000 concurrent requests, 120 s measured after a 30 s warm-up, server capped at 1 to 4 CPUs and 4096m RAM, run at grpc_bench commit c4c93b3 (2026-04-22)
claimed_speedup: Discussion #559 (2026-04-23 run), java_armeria vs cpp_grpc_mt in req/s: 1 CPU 56315 vs 57403 (0.98x, C++ ahead); 2 CPUs 95471 vs 74574 (1.28x); 3 CPUs 134838 vs 81581 (1.65x); 4 CPUs 140386 vs 85485 (1.64x) (ratios derived from page data). Average latency at 4 CPUs 5.25 ms vs 11.28 ms; average CPU 330.65% vs 405.58% at 4 CPUs.
compiler_and_flags: Server under test (Dockerfile at c4c93b3, unchanged at HEAD): eclipse-temurin:23-jdk-noble, JAVA_OPTS -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MinRAMPercentage=70 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -Dcom.linecorp.armeria.validateHeaders=false; armeria 1.20.3 with grpc-java 1.58.0 and protoc 3.21.5 built by gradlew installDist; the server code calls disableDateHeader() and disableServerHeader(). Baseline cpp_grpc_mt at commit c4c93b3: FROM gcc:15.2.0, g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto main.cpp gen/*.cc -lgrpc++ -lprotobuf -lgrpc -lgpr -lpthread -ljemalloc; libgrpc++-dev, protobuf and libjemalloc come from Debian packages (versions and build flags not stated).
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (16) @ 2.800GHz, 64 GB RAM, Digital Ocean dedicated server, Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-71-generic; server limited by Docker to 1, 2, 3 or 4 CPUs, ghz 0.114.0 client given 11 CPUs
why_faster: No source gives a mechanism (the grpc_bench README and discussion only report numbers). Inference from the same tables: at 4 CPUs the C++ server used 405.58% CPU for 85485 req/s while Armeria used 330.65% for 140386 req/s, so the gap is cost per request, not idle CPU; the cause (gRPC C++ completion-queue overhead against Netty event loops and JIT-compiled code) is not established.
tradeoffs: Memory: 570.43 to 678.56 MiB average for Armeria against 20.59 to 31.71 MiB for the C++ server in the same run (about 21 to 28x more). JVM warm-up (the suite uses a 30 s warm-up) and G1GC; gRPC-Java stack with Netty underneath; the C++ server needs no runtime.
caveats: The win is not stable across the suite's own published runs. Other published grpc_bench result threads that I opened (ratios derived from page data): #441 (i9-13900KF, 2024-04, commit e64db6d) armeria/cpp_grpc_mt = 0.71, 0.72, 0.80, 0.82, 0.84, 0.92 at 1 to 6 server CPUs; #475 (i5-6600K, 2024-09, commit 38875a7) 0.03 (1138 req/s, an apparent 1-CPU JVM anomaly), 0.48, 0.84, 0.87 at 1 to 4 CPUs; #547 (Ryzen 9 5900X, 2025-12) 0.92, 0.97, 1.02 at 1, 4 and 24 CPUs. Armeria is clearly ahead only in the April 2026 Xeon run (2 to 4 CPUs) and behind at 1 CPU there. One run per CPU count, no variance, results posted by the suite maintainer rather than the Armeria authors. The server is tuned for the benchmark (Date and Server headers off, header validation off, 70% heap), while the C++ server is the plain gRPC async pattern on distro libgrpc. The build pins armeria 1.20.3 and grpc-java 1.58.0 (the project is at release 1.42.0 on 2026-10-06), so the rows do not describe current Armeria. cpu and memory columns come from docker stats. The Dockerfile I read at HEAD for the C++ side says gcc:16.1.0; the run used gcc:15.2.0.

name: vlagent (Go log collector, VictoriaLogs): log-collectors-benchmark vs Fluent Bit
baseline: Fluent Bit (C), v5.0.9 in the 2026-09-17 run (v4.2.3 in the 2026-08-12 and 2026-09-16 runs), Helm chart fluent/fluent-bit 0.57.9, tail input with the kubernetes filter and an HTTP JSON-lines output with gzip, limited to 1 CPU and 1 GiB
workload: Kubernetes log collection on a local kind cluster: (a) resources case, 10 log-generator Pods at 1000 JSON lines per second each (about 10k logs/s) for one hour, measuring average CPU and memory; (b) maximum-throughput case, 50 Pods starting at 50 logs/s each and adding 20 logs/s per Pod every 10 s until throughput stops growing; both ship to a log-verifier that counts lost lines; each collector limited to 1 CPU and 1 GiB
claimed_speedup: results/2026-09-17 (vlagent v1.52.0 vs Fluent Bit v5.0.9): resources case average CPU 0.0476 vs 0.2040 cores (4.3x less, derived from page data), average memory 33152688 vs 56061519 bytes (1.7x less, derived), max memory 46620672 vs 110538752 bytes, lost 0 vs 3; throughput case 177949 vs 41222 logs/s (4.3x, derived), where the Fluent Bit run is marked Success false, FailReason OOMKilled, Lost 1133131. The 2026-08-12 run (vlagent v1.48.0, Fluent Bit v4.2.3) gives 178274 vs 40218 logs/s and CPU 0.0479 vs 0.2116 cores; the 2026-09-16 run gives 176712 vs 39734 logs/s and CPU 0.0478 vs 0.2131 cores.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt release images from Helm charts (vm/victoria-logs-collector 0.3.7 for vlagent, fluent/fluent-bit 0.57.9), no compiler flags. Fluent Bit config in values/fluent-bit.yml: tail input (Skip_Long_Lines On, docker and cri multiline parsers), kubernetes filter (Merge_Log On, Keep_Log Off), http output (json_lines, gzip). vlagent uses jsonline output with includeNodeLabels.
hardware: Not stated in the repo or its README (single host running a kind cluster; the README says running all collectors at once needs at least 12 CPUs, 12 GiB RAM and 200 GiB disk). A web-search summary of a secondary write-up of the original blog (not opened) says that blog ran all collectors concurrently on one 32-CPU VM; unverified, CPU model unknown.
why_faster: Not given in the repo or README. The only related note is in values/vlagent.yml: vlagent's native VictoriaLogs format would use about 20% less CPU than the jsonline format chosen for a fair comparison with the other collectors.
stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars (VictoriaLogs repo; vlagent lives in app/vlagent); benchmark repo 29 stars
tradeoffs: vlagent is a Go program that lives inside the VictoriaLogs repository (app/vlagent) and targets VictoriaLogs-compatible insert APIs; Fluent Bit supports many more inputs, filters and outputs. In the one-hour resources case vlagent also uses less memory (31.6 MiB average against 53.5 MiB, derived).
caveats: First-party benchmark: VictoriaMetrics runs the suite and sells VictoriaLogs, so the tier is capped at C. Hardware is not stated. The Fluent Bit throughput run failed in all three committed rounds (OOMKilled, 252175 to 1133131 lines lost), so 41222 logs/s is the point of failure, not a clean capacity figure; the maintainers added Mem_Buf_Limit 512MB to the tail input on 2026-09-23 (commit c53524a) and no post-fix results are committed. Fluent Bit uses an untuned configuration close to the Helm chart defaults (no worker threads or batch tuning), and the README invites tuning PRs. Each collector is limited to 1 CPU, which favours a light agent. The 2026-09-16 and 2026-09-17 rounds were committed together to show node configuration did not change results (commit 31266d0). The published results page and blog post are on blocked hosts, so numbers here come from the committed JSON files only. One run per round per case.

name: Dart AOT 3.13.0: benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: README table of 3 September 2026, binary trees: Dart (3.13.0 AOT) 0.865 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s, about 1.17x faster than C and 1.33x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Dart loses overall: total 20.754 s against 9.762 s for C (2.13x slower), with Fibonacci 8.135 s vs 1.694 s and strings 6.523 s vs 2.132 s.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable, flake.lock pinned). Dart: dart compile exe bench.dart -o bench -S bench.sym (AOT, runtime embedded; no optimization switches used).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux with i3-wm, one run per language on 2026-09-03
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump allocation in the Dart young generation and cheap scavenges of short-lived trees against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 74.6 MiB for Dart against 33.3 MiB for C; stripped executable 5617 KiB against 26 KiB (the AOT binary embeds the runtime). Dart is slower than C on primes (2.963 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci and strings.
caveats: The Dart source is not in the repository: .gitignore ignores every file and whitelists extensions language by language (*.c, *.cpp, *.d, *.java and so on) with no rule for *.dart, the languages/ directory listing on GitHub has no Dart folder, and raw.githubusercontent.com returns 404 for languages/Dart/bench.dart although run_benchmarks.sh runs it from there. The Dart row therefore cannot be reproduced or inspected, so the tier is C although the suite is otherwise public; same_algorithm is null because only the analyzer's checksum comparison supports it. One run per language (no variance), single machine. The C and C++ programs are naive per-node malloc/free (I read languages/C/bench.c and languages/C++/bench.cpp); an arena or pool allocator in C would beat the runtimes here. This is 1 of 5 workloads, and C wins overall. Managed runtimes keep default settings with JIT or GC threads and the C code frees inside the timer while the GC need not collect, the same harness effect that puts Java (0.347 s), Nim (0.809 s), Bun (0.816 s), OCaml (0.865 s) and C# (0.931 s) ahead of C on this row.

name: Free Pascal 3.2.2: compile throughput in nordlow/compiler-benchmark
baseline: C (gcc-15 15.3.0, gcc 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and C++ (g++-15 15.3.0, g++ 16.2.1, clang++ 23.1.1) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit (200 call chains of depth 200, 40000 functions) with default optimization (no -O flag)
workload: Microseconds per function to build (compile plus link) and to compile only a single generated file of 200 x 200 trivial Int64 add-chains; the 'Total' column is build plus a run of the resulting binary, the 'Compile' column is object-only
claimed_speedup: README table: Free Pascal (fpc 3.2.2) Total 138 us/f (137 build + 0.20 run) and Compile 103.6 us/f, against C (gcc-15 15.3.0) 392 Total and 193.8 Compile, C (gcc 16.2.1) 454 Total and 400.1 Compile, C++ (g++-15) 303 Total, C++ (g++ 16.2.1) 486 Total, C++ (clang++ 23.1.1) 236 Total. About 2.8x faster than gcc-15 Total, 3.3x than gcc 16.2.1 and 1.7x than clang++ (derived from page data). C (clang 23.1.1) is faster than Free Pascal: 118 Total and 77.9 Compile.
compiler_and_flags: cbench script, fpc: build 'fpc -O- -B -Aas -o<bin>' (no optimization, rebuild all, GNU assembler), compile 'fpc -Cn -O-'. gcc and g++: 'gcc -Wall -Wextra -o <bin> main.c', 'g++ -Wno-c++11-extensions', compile with -c, i.e. the default optimization level (-O0) with warnings enabled for C; clang the same with extra diagnostics flags. Linker not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09; one worker per core, tasks pinned with sched_setaffinity and run in parallel, minimum of up to 10 runs
why_faster: The README attributes fast compile speed to compiler architecture (single translation unit of arithmetic chains, no header parsing) but gives no Pascal-specific explanation. Inference: Free Pascal's unit system needs no preprocessing or textual includes and it builds with -O-.
stars_or_usage: benchmark repo 167 stars; Free Pascal is a long-established compiler (GitLab project, 75386 commits)
tradeoffs: The generated Pascal binary is the most compact of the table (68.8 bytes per function against 121.1 for gcc) but the optimizing-compile cost is not measured: every compiler runs unoptimized. Check-only mode costs 98.7 us/f, close to its full compile, because fpc has no cheap syntax-only pass.
caveats: The workload is one synthetic 40000-function translation unit of arithmetic with no includes, standard library or optimization, so it does not predict real project build times; at -O2 or -O3 the gcc and clang numbers would be much larger and Free Pascal's -O- row would not be a like-for-like release build. The C compilers are run with -Wall -Wextra (C) and warnings diagnostics that fpc does not get. The Total column adds the run time of the produced binary (0.10 to 0.21 us/f, clang C shows 1.2) and includes linking; the linker used is not stated, Free Pascal is forced to the external GNU assembler by -Aas, while Zig is run with -fno-llvm -fno-lld (own backend and linker) and DMD uses its own backend, so linking work is not uniform across rows; the sibling Zig, Odin, Rust, C3 and D records in this wave say the README documents no flags and are tiered B, but the cbench script does document them. clang is faster than Free Pascal (118 against 138 Total). Run-to-run movement on the same machine is large (see below). Parallel pinned workers share caches and memory bandwidth. Both Pascal and Hare sit in the README's 'Modern Systems Languages' table. The README's Conclusions section quotes older numbers than its own table (clang 87 us/f against 118 in the table, gcc 418 to 455 against 392 to 454), which shows how much the same machine's results move between samples.

name: dg2d (D 2D vector rasterizer, cerjones)
baseline: Cairo (C) and Blend2D (C++), named only in the orchestrator's lead; the repository names no baseline
workload: 2D path rasterization with SIMD (SSE2) into 32 bits-per-pixel buffers; no benchmark is published

name: zeebo/xxh3 (Go XXH3 with assembly)
baseline: xxHash XXH3 (C reference implementation by Cyan4973), not benchmarked in the repository
workload: XXH3 64-bit and 128-bit hashing of 0 to 100 KB inputs in Go, with SSE2, AVX2, AVX512 (amd64) and NEON (arm64) assembly accumulators; benchmark tables report Go results only
claimed_speedup: none against C: the README tables report Go throughput only, e.g. AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 64-bit hash of 100KB 4.03 us/op (25.4 GB/s) in the plain Rate column (not defined in the README, apparently the non-assembly path), 2.10 us/op (48.7 GB/s) SSE2, 1.07 us/op (96.0 GB/s) AVX2, 685 ns/op (149 GB/s) AVX512; Intel i7-8850H @ 2.60GHz 100KB 13.0 us/op (7.88 GB/s) plain Rate, 4.05 us/op (25.3 GB/s) SSE2, 2.31 us/op (44.3 GB/s) AVX2.
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain with assembly accumulators (an avo directory is present in the repo); Go version and build flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X and Intel i7-8850H @ 2.60GHz (README benchmark headings)
tradeoffs: Assembly only for amd64 and arm64 (other platforms use the portable Go path; on the i7-8850H the plain Rate column is 7.88 GB/s at 100KB against 44.3 GB/s in the AVX2 column); a non-zero seed re-derives the 192-byte secret on every call so seeded hashing is slower at small sizes (512 B SSE2: 20.3 against 11.2 ns/op).
caveats: The orchestrator's lead said the README compares against the C implementation through cgo; it does not. The README has Go-only tables, internal/compare/compare_test.go benchmarks against cespare/xxhash (a Go XXH64 implementation), and _compat.c plus compat_test.go use the C library only to generate and check test vectors for correctness. No C-versus-Go timing exists in the repository, so this stays a tier D record and does not support a claim against the C baseline. go-simd/xxhash's README compares itself with zeebo/xxh3, also without a C baseline.
